//platform: The platform base URLs are placeholders on purpose. A reachable endpoint is deployment data and does not belong in a repository, so the host is filled in from the environment — see .env.example. The paths are the platform's own API shape and are kept.
//imports: An operator can take an import as an input the way it takes a device, and an import type carries the same content variables a device type does. device_selection_url is the discovery half: empty means semantic selection reports devices only, and says so in its notes rather than implying the platform has no imports. It is deliberately not used for devices — its device answer drops the connection state, the device type name and the full device type, and hard-codes `shared` to false, so ODE would have to read the devices again anyway. Setting it requires import_deploy_url, because discovery carries no container status and a stopped import would otherwise be indistinguishable from a live one. import_repo_url is the import type catalogue, and it is not optional in the way it looks: discovery joins every matching type to its instances and reports one row per instance, so a type nobody has deployed yet is invisible to it — and that is exactly the type create_import_instance exists for. Without this, get_import_type_metadata and list_import_types refuse, a resolution reports no deployable_import_types, and an empty import half cannot say whether the platform describes the wanted signal at all. analytics_serving_url is how a live-only import is told from an exported one: timescale-wrapper has no importId and there is no table worker for imports, so an import's history exists only if an export was created for it — without this the question answers `unknown`, which is honest and different from `no history`.
//simulation: MOSES, the platform's environment simulator, as ODE's source of test scenarios. An operator needs data before it can be developed, and the data it needs is rarely there on the day the work starts — a forecast wants weeks of history, a cycle detector wants a machine that cycles, a submetering operator wants a meter tree with something under it. MOSES simulates the site instead, and because a simulated asset is an ordinary platform device the rest of ODE already finds what one publishes. Empty moses_url leaves the fourteen simulation tools declared-but-unavailable, the same degradation an empty ray_url does; nothing in ODE requires a simulator. There is no token here and never will be: MOSES takes an environment's owner from the caller's token, so a service account would create simulations belonging to ODE that nobody could find and nobody could delete. moses_request_timeout is generous by metadata standards because storing an environment registers a platform device per new asset, one call each, before MOSES answers at all. moses_max_dataset_bytes bounds one uploaded timeseries — a bound on ODE's own memory, since the file travels out of the developer's pod base64-encoded and then through ODE whole, and a file over it is refused rather than uploaded truncated, because a cut-off CSV parses and then plays silence from wherever it was cut.
//exports: The four fields of an export that belong to this deployment rather than to the import being exported, used by create_export. export_offset is where the export worker starts reading: `smallest` takes what the Kafka topic still retains, `largest` only what arrives from now on, and the assistant may choose between the two per export. export_time_path is where the timestamp sits in an import message, which is `time` beside the `value` payload for every import type; an import whose values describe a time other than their arrival — a backfill, a forecast — overrides it per export, because that is a property of the import type and not of this deployment. The two empty ones are not defaults: export_timestamp_format is whatever this platform's export worker parses and export_database_id is minted by analytics-serving's own migration, so neither can be derived — left empty, ODE copies them from an export this platform already has, and refuses to create one rather than guessing when there is nothing to copy.
//profiler_raw_window_points: Bounds the raw pass's response, not its rows: the read is one wide row per message carrying one value per variable, so this figure is divided by the variables read (floored at 2000 rows) and the applied number is recorded in the profile as raw_window.row_limit.
//postgres: Empty runs the in-memory stores. A per-user LLM spend cap is then only as old as the process, so set this before relying on one (§3.3).
//llm: Any subset of the four providers of §5.7. With none configured, ODE serves the ontology, selection and profiler surfaces and no chat. Keys belong in the environment, not here.
//claude_cli: A development convenience for working without an API key. Reaches ODE's tools over MCP, so it needs public_url to be set. claude_cli_timeout bounds one turn, which for this provider is a whole agent loop rather than one model call: it is the ceiling a held confirmation has to fit inside, and a turn that reaches it is stopped with SIGKILL and reported as having reached its ceiling. It has to stay under chat_exchange_timeout, which bounds the exchange carrying the turn — startup warns when it does not. Empty takes the ten minutes in llm.DefaultCLITimeout.
//chat_confirmation_timeout: How long a tool call that needs the developer's confirmation (D11) is held open waiting for their answer. It only applies where a provider runs its own tool loop, which today means the CLI above: the call blocks on ODE's side while the card is on screen, and the decision becomes its result. It is not chat_exchange_timeout, which bounds the whole turn, and it has to stay well under the CLI's own ten-minute turn timeout — a turn that ends underneath the card leaves an approval with nothing to run into. Startup warns when it does not.
//chat_exchange_timeout: Bounds one detached exchange: everything one message sets off, including the whole tool loop. It is the outer bound on a turn rather than a turn's own ceiling, so it has to stay above claude_cli_timeout — a CLI ceiling above this one can never be reached, because the exchange ends first and takes the turn with it. Empty takes 30m.
//llm_pricing: Per million tokens, for the estimated cost §3.3 accounts against. Matched exactly, else by longest prefix. Not baked into the binary: published prices change, and a stale figure makes a cost cap quietly wrong. Verify before relying on these.
//jupyterhub: §5.6. Empty leaves the kernel surface unserved. The token is ODE's JupyterHub *service* credential and must hold servers, tokens, access:servers and users:activity — startup fails if it does not. Granting them is deployment configuration and is not part of this repository. The workspace path is relative to the singleuser server root and has to be inside the mounted PVC, which is why the default sits under data/ rather than at the home root.
//tool_bounds: The first two bound one projection; the next two bound a whole response. tool_quick_token_budget is what a ranked candidate list may cost the model, tool_profile_max_profiles how many full profiles one profile_series answer carries. Raise them and every tool call carries the difference for the rest of the turn.
//charts: §5.9. chart_max_points bounds one series of one chart: the aggregation bucket is widened until the window fits it, so this trades resolution against the size of the read and never truncates the window. chart_default_lookback is what a chart covers when neither the author nor a named profile says.
//relations: §5.5. relation_max_members bounds one relational pass; the pair count grows with the square of it and the rule count with four times that, so this bounds how readable the rule list is rather than how expensive the read is — the aligned read is one batched query either way. relation_max_buckets bounds the aligned grid, which is widened to fit rather than shortening the window. relation_default_lookback is a month rather than a week because an exception at certain times of day needs several samples in each hour bucket of each weekday. relation_max_graph_neighbours bounds how far out of the requested aspect a device relationship graph may pull: a graph of a whole site names hundreds of devices, and each one outside the aspect costs a device read, so this is what keeps one room's question from becoming a site survey.
//github: §5.11. Empty github_client_id leaves the repo surface unserved and write_file declared-but-unavailable; the surface also needs a jupyterhub_url, because the working copy lives on the developer's pod. github_token_key is required when a client id is set — the developer's GitHub token is stored encrypted (item 1) — and is base64 of 32 bytes: `openssl rand -base64 32`. The secret and the key belong in the environment, not here. github_redirect_uri is the *SPA's* callback and has to match the OAuth app's registered one exactly; empty derives it from public_url, which is right only when ODE serves the SPA itself.
//repo: repo_command_timeout bounds one git command, and is minutes because a clone of a repository with history is the slow one. repo_max_file_bytes bounds a file the Code pane or write_file may move in one request. repo_max_workbenches caps how many working contexts a developer may hold open; each one is a kernel process in their pod, so this figure and the memory on the KubeSpawner profile have to be raised together. operator_lib_ref empty resolves the newest tag at scaffold time and records it per repository, which is D15's `track latest, pin per repo`; setting it fixes every new repository to one ref.
//experiments: §5.12. Empty ray_url or mlflow_url leaves the experiment routes unserved and launch_experiment and get_experiment_results declared-but-unavailable; setting one without the other fails startup, because ODE creates the MLflow run before submitting the job and a cluster without a tracking server cannot launch anything. The surface also needs a jupyterhub_url and a github_client_id: the job package is `git archive` of the developer's *committed* working copy, and that copy lives on their pod. ray_url and mlflow_url are the API bases ODE calls; ray_dashboard_url and mlflow_ui_url are what a browser should open, which in a cluster is routinely a different host — they are what the embed probe of D6 asks and what the pane links to, and empty falls back to the API base. The two tokens are the service accounts §3.1 item 5 permits, the only place in ODE where one is legitimate, and both may be empty because an in-cluster dashboard is commonly unauthenticated and M10's NetworkPolicy is what bounds who reaches it. They belong in the environment, not here.
//experiment_deployment_config: A run takes the operator's own training path: ODE hands the job Operator Lib's deployment config, and MLOperator opens the MLflow run, connects to Ray, calls train() and registers the model. These three are what that config carries. experiment_ray_client_url is what Operator Lib passes to ray.init() and is NOT ray_url, which is the dashboard ODE submits jobs to over HTTP -- 'auto' attaches to the cluster the driver already runs in, while a deployed operator names the cluster's client endpoint because it connects from outside. experiment_ts_conn is the timescale DSN provide_historic_data reads history through; it is a shared database credential rather than the caller's token, it reaches every series, and which series a run reads is decided by its input topics rather than by who launched it -- acceptable while every developer is team-internal with platform administration rights, and tracked as SNRGY-4637. experiment_kafka_bootstrap is only needed for an input topic replayed from Kafka rather than read from timescale; empty leaves a run able to train from timescale-backed topics only.
//experiment_bounds: experiment_max_package_bytes bounds the job archive, and exceeding it is *reported rather than truncated*: a job that ran against a partial repository fails in a way nobody could diagnose from the run. It also bounds ODE's own memory, because the archive is held whole and travels back from the pod base64-encoded, which costs a third more again. 16 MiB is three orders of magnitude more than a source repository needs; what it actually catches is a checked-in model file or a data directory. The two env bounds matter because a launch arrives from an HTTP body or from an LLM tool call, and neither is trusted input. experiment_max_log_bytes bounds the developer's own log route — logs never reach a model (§5.13).
//experiment_timeouts: experiment_request_timeout bounds one Ray or MLflow API call; experiment_upload_timeout bounds the one request that moves the whole archive, and is separate for the reason the profiler's two read timeouts are separate — a bound that fits a status probe cannot fit a multi-megabyte upload, and one figure for both means either the probe hangs or the upload is cut off mid-body. The embed pair is D6's: how long a framing verdict is cached, and how long one probe may take. The probe timeout is short on purpose, because an unreachable service is a normal answer there and the pane is waiting for it.
//result_interpretation:
§5.13. This is what makes a finished run reach the conversation it came from without anyone watching. experiment_poll_interval is how often ODE asks Ray about the runs it still calls unfinished — a status refreshed only when somebody looked was right while nothing acted on a status change, and is not right once §5.13 does. experiment_poll_window is how far back a finished run is still offered for interpretation, and it is not a tuning knob: it is the figure that covers an ODE restart. A deployment that was down for an hour should still interpret the runs that finished during it, and one that has been down for a week should not replay the week into every developer's conversation on the first tick. experiment_poll_batch caps how many records one tick touches and experiment_poll_timeout bounds the whole tick, so a Ray dashboard that has stopped answering costs one tick rather than the loop.

interpretation_retry_interval is how often the runs waiting for a developer are tried again. Every reason an automated turn is refused is transient — the session is already running an exchange, the §3.3 spend cap has not reset, the developer has not come back — so this is the interval at which those resolve rather than a backoff. interpretation_turn_timeout bounds how long one turn is *waited for*, not how long it may run: chat_exchange_timeout is the real ceiling, and abandoning a turn the developer is watching in order to record its proposal on time would be the wrong trade. interpretation_max_pending bounds the summaries held for developers who are away, so a cluster that finished a thousand jobs overnight does not become a thousand held documents.

None of these buys ODE a credential. The summary is built with the Ray and MLflow service accounts §3.1 item 5 permits; the interpretation turn runs only while a developer is connected and presenting their own token, because it dispatches tools and every platform read is on their behalf (§3.1 item 3). That is why a run can be summarised at three in the morning and interpreted at nine, and why the evaluation criteria in the summary say `no_developer_credential` until then rather than reporting a criterion as unmet.
//job_token: §3.1 item 6, and the risk register's `token expiry vs. long Ray jobs` row. A Ray job reads its training data from timescale-wrapper directly with its own token (§5.3.4) and a training run outlives an interactive session, so where these four are set ODE mints one token per submission through an RFC 8693 token exchange, on behalf of the developer — the job's authorisation stays theirs, which a service account would have violated. Where they are not set ODE degrades the way the rest of ODE degrades: the caller's session token is passed, a warning at startup names what is missing, and every launch result says the credential expires with the session. job_token_audience is not optional in practice, because Keycloak returns a token for the *requesting* client unless an audience names another and a job reads timescale-wrapper. job_token_lifetime is an expectation rather than a request: neither RFC 8693 nor Keycloak accepts a requested lifetime, so ODE compares it against the issuer's own expires_in and warns on a shortfall. The secret belongs in the environment, not here.
//tool_run_code: Far smaller than jupyterhub_max_output_bytes above, and for a different cost: that one bounds a developer's console, this one bounds what a cell's output costs in model context.
